haiku-low.q1: Keys load before the HTTP server starts. /healthz returns 200 only once the snapshot holds all three keys, so the instance is marked ready after loading.
haiku-low.q2: It retries missing secrets up to 4 attempts, then logs an error and exits non-zero. It never becomes ready, so the rollout halts and old pods keep serving traffic.
haiku-low.q3: A refresher thread fetches each secret every 5 minutes and swaps in new versions atomically. On failure it keeps the previous value, logs a WARNING, and stays ready.
haiku-low.q4: Key values live only in process memory, in the secrets snapshot. They must never appear on disk, in environment variables, or in logs.
haiku-low.q5: Only the security on-call group can write prod secrets. Engineers cannot read prod values. The orders-api-prod identity has read-only access to prod paths.
haiku-low.q6: The old keys sat in git history for two years, so they are treated as leaked. Each is rotated at its provider and revoked, which makes the old values useless.
haiku-low.q7: Clients hold a reference to the secrets provider and call get(name) on every request. Each call reads the current snapshot, so the new key is used on the next call.
haiku-low.q8: Check that every pod runs the new image, each pod's latest secrets_refreshed line shows expected version ids, and old-key last-used times are stale with no unknown callers.
haiku-low.q9: Document order: store access (step 2), issue new provider keys (3), write them to store (4), code change removing YAML keys (5), rollout (7), then revoke old keys (10).
haiku-low.q10: Dev paths orders-api/dev/* with the engineer's own login, using provider sandbox keys. make run-offline uses a fake backend with placeholder values instead.
haiku-low.q11: It retries only the missing secret, up to 4 attempts total. If it still fails, it logs an error naming the secrets and exits non-zero, never becoming ready.
haiku-low.q12: NOT STATED. The plan picks no rotation cadence; security has not decided whether or how often keys must be rotated on a schedule.

sonnet.q1: Keys are loaded first. The HTTP server does not start until all three keys load. /healthz returns 200 only while the snapshot holds all three, so the instance is ready only after loading.
sonnet.q2: It retries (2s wait, up to 3 retries, 4 attempts), then exits non-zero and never becomes ready. The rollout halts and old pods keep serving, so live traffic is unaffected.
sonnet.q3: A refresher thread fetches the latest version of each secret every 5 minutes. A new version id goes into a new snapshot that is swapped in atomically. On a fetch error it keeps the previous value, logs a WARNING (no values), and readiness stays 200. Other secrets still update, and the on-call is alerted if no cycle succeeds for several cycles. A provider 401 or 403 can also trigger a forced re-read of that one secret.
sonnet.q4: Held in process heap memory only, as Secret wrappers in the snapshot. They must never be on disk, in env vars, in logs or in core dumps (disabled). Printing a Secret shows <redacted>.
sonnet.q5: Only the security on-call group can write prod secrets. Engineers cannot read prod values. The orders-api-prod pod identity has read-only access to orders-api/prod/*. The doc does not name any human who can read prod values.
sonnet.q6: The keys remain in git history for two years and in old container images, so they are treated as leaked. They are made harmless by rotating every key at its provider, with the old keys revoked only after the confirmation gate passes.
sonnet.q7: Clients hold a reference to the secrets provider, not a key value. On every call they use secrets.get(name) to read the current snapshot's key and call reveal(). A request already in flight keeps the value it read.
sonnet.q8: A three-part gate recorded in the ticket. (1) Every pod, job and script in every environment runs the new image digest. (2) Each live pod's latest secrets_refreshed log line shows the expected version ids, grouped by pod name and compared with the pod list, and a stale line fails. (3) Each provider shows the old key's last-used time older than one refresh interval plus a margin, with no unknown callers.
sonnet.q9: Rollout order: 1 inventory and provider check; 2 store layout and access policies; 3 issue new keys at providers; 4 write the keys into the store; 5 build and review the code change (which removes the keys from the YAML; it may be written any time but must not merge before step 4); 6 staging deploy and drills; 7 prod rolling deploy; 8 gate; 9 block old images; 10 revoke old keys. Rotation (new keys issued) comes before the app switches, and revocation of the old keys is last.
sonnet.q10: From the secret store under orders-api/dev/*, using the engineer's own login. These paths hold provider sandbox keys. Alternatively, make run-offline uses a fake in-process backend with placeholder values.
sonnet.q11: It treats this as a failed fetch for the missing secret. It retries only the missing one (2s wait, up to 3 retries). If it is still missing, it logs an error naming the secret and the error class and exits non-zero, so the server never starts.
sonnet.q12: NOT STATED. Rotation cadence is an open question owned by security. The plan picks no schedule, though the mechanism supports any cadence.
